utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, Julian Nicholls, and Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic for Mr. Brdjanin. And the LiveNote is not working on either of our systems here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It wasn't working on mine either, but when I pressed "Video," it started work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. Maybe that will do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have further problems, let me know, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's working on the monitor but not on the small --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the small one I think you have to make sure that you are connected. The system is definitely on. Maybe you're not connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll try to reconnect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the laptop -- Madam Chuqing, is the laptop on the front desk working?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This one is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And ours are not working, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think I'll call in the technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, everyone has got the main screen working. But whether the others are working or not perhaps is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is not completely correct, Ms. Korner, because I do watch what is happening in the courtroom, and many a time I have seen Mr. Ackerman blocking and then copying or mark --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sure he is, Your Honour. But that -- that may be right, but it's not vital for this hearing to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him say whether it's vital for him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think because this one is working -- the only reason that we would need it today, I would think, is to be able to download a transcript at the close of today's -- and as long as that's working, we can do it from that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's probably okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will proceed. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you. For the record, the Trial Chamber notices that General Talic is not present. And for the record also, I'm going to read out a waiver that the Chamber has been provided with signed by General Momir Talic and dated today, on the 17th of September. I'm going to read it in English, and this is what it states: "I, Momir Talic, am willingly signing this waiver which is being presented to me. I am aware of my right to consult my lawyer in this matter. I have not been coerced or forced to sign this. I waive my right to be present at the court proceedings on Tuesday, 17 September 2002. Signed, The Hague, 17 September, Momir Talic." So that's for the record. Before we start, are there any preliminaries that you would like to discuss?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, only one -- well, they're related matters. First of all, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I suggest that in the light of the Defence application to lift the confidentiality and indeed in respect of some reporting that has taken place, which I wish to raise with Your Honour at the end of the hearing, because it is a disgrace that it is -- what was purported to be said in closed session was published in the newspaper. But Your Honour, it seems to me that unless there's an objection from either Defence counsel - and I think there probably won't be - that the proceedings should continue in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact -- Mr. Zecevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have any objection, Your Honour, to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I suppose you don't either, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I was going to propose to you today, as precisely a first step, before we embark on the debate on the provisional release, that we will remain throughout in open session. At this point in time, having already dealt with the details of General Talic's present state of health in closed session, there is no further reason why we should remain in closed session. And let's take certain preliminary items on today's sort of agenda one by one. There is a motion which you've just referred to, Ms. Korner, a motion by the Defence team for General Talic asking this Trial Chamber to lift the confidentiality that it had already decided upon, relating to the previous proceedings on general -- on the motion for provisional release, which hasn't been debated as of yet, but on what was debated here in closed session on General Talic's health situation, condition, as well as what followed afterwards; in other words, the Prosecution motion for an adjournment of the proceedings till today. Do you maintain your position? Do you maintain your motion for the lifting of the confidentiality veil?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any objection on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To the contrary, Your Honour. And I think it ought to be made clear, because there's been a lot of complaints from the Defence side about the Prosecution request for closed session. All of the closed session hearings, the confidentiality of the motions were at the request of the Defence, for what obviously then are understandable reasons. Your Honour, we clearly don't oppose that. Your Honour, we filed our response to the Defence motion for seeking provisional release confidentiality because at that stage there had been no order lifting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And now, this is what I'm coming to. As a logical consequence, the motion -- or rather, your response to the motion for the provisional release, which you filed confidentially and which was handed to us earlier on today at about half past 12.00, need no longer or cannot logically remain confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour, because at that stage the motion for provisional release was still confidential, so we had to reply confidentially. We have absolutely no objection to the lifting of the confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the first decision that we are taking, Madam Registrar - and this is an oral decision - is that the motion for provisional release filed by General Talic - and I'm sure you will find the date - you'll spare me having to give you the date myself - the Prosecution's response to that motion, which was filed today, and the proceedings on General Talic's motion, including the proceedings in the course of which evidence was heard on General Talic's state -- present state of health, will no longer remain confidential, even though those proceedings were held in closed session. That's the first decision that is being taken. The second matter that I would like to have you discuss and which should engage us in not more than a few minutes is a request or a motion that has been filed in French by the Defence team for General Talic in which -- or by means of which this Chamber is being requested to give ear ad wit in a room and hear with the representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia relative to the motion that is before this Chamber for the provisional release of General Talic. Is there any objection on the part of the Prosecution for admitting in the courtroom a representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and hearing -- receiving his testimony, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: None at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that is, therefore, the decision -- the second decision that this Chamber is taking. In other words, the motion by General Talic dated yesterday, 16th September, namely, "Requete aux fins d'admission d'un temoin," is being accepted and we will tell you when to admit the representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The third point I wanted to clarify is actually a direct question to Mr. Zecevic. I would imagine that you were -- that you received the Prosecution's response more or less about the same time that we did. Did you have time -- enough time to read it and consider it? Are you prepared to make submissions on it, or would you like some kind of postponement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No postponement, Your Honour. Thank you for asking. But we are ready to give submissions on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should add that we had a meeting this morning, and I spoke to Madam Fauveau yesterday, so I gave the general gist of what our attitude was going to be in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So at this point in time I think the way I would suggest to you to proceed is rather than asking Mr. Zecevic to explain the rationale, the basis for his motion for provisional release of General Talic, I would turn on to you on the basis of the response that you have filed today and ask you to elaborate, Ms. Korner, and then obviously I will give the floor to Mr. Zecevic and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would help if Your Honour would -- would say in what way you wanted us to elaborate. We've set our position, we thought, fairly clearly -- we hoped fairly clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think very simply put, there is a part in your response which I would require elaboration upon. And this is where you say: "The Pre-Trial --" paragraph number 4, last sentence: "The Pre-Trial Chamber's rationale for ordering the detention of Talic before and during the trial has not evaporated simply because his health has deteriorated." Correct. The Chamber would agree completely with that affirmation. Then you move on to paragraph 5: "The public perception of such a provisional release could be extremely damaging to the institutional authority of the Prosecutor and her ability to conduct investigations in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and the subsequent trials in The Hague. Victims and other witnesses who have agreed to cooperate with the Prosecution will not have a favourable view of the provisional release of Talic whatever the circumstances. On the contrary, in the context of their own suffering they will not understand the humanitarian motivation behind such a release. The Prosecutor therefore proposes an alternative strategy." And according to you this strategy "accommodates the need for Talic to be transferred to the FRY, to receive whatever treatment he may wish or require, but also recognises the fact that Talic is an accused under arrest in an ongoing trial who prima facie is responsible for the death and suffering of thousands of Muslims," et cetera. How -- then you propose that Talic remains in detention, however not in the detention unit here in The Hague, but will remain in detention in Belgrade, in the hospital where he will receive treatment, irrespective of whether he's receiving treatment at the time or not, because we have heard from the doctors that if he receives chemotherapy, for example, usually you -- you go for chemotherapy, you stay two hours in the hospital, and you're out. And you are expecting this Trial Chamber to place an order on the authorities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, particularly the hospital -- the military hospital in that capital, ensuring that they will substitute for all intensive purposes the role of the United Nations Detention Unit here in The Hague for the purposes of the detention of accused Talic and stay there for as long as Mr. Talic -- General Talic requires treatment or independently of treatment, as long as he is still unfit to return to this Tribunal or to be in detention in -- here in The Hague. How would that change the perception of the persons, the victims in particular, and witnesses, because for all intents and purposes General Talic will not be here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still have an ongoing trial, but he is going to be in a hospital in -- call it detention, call it whatever you like, but how is the public perception going to change?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First can I just add one thing: Clearly all of this would be dependent on the agreement of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We have been in contact -- not the gentleman who's here today. I don't know what his status is nor indeed his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I doubt if he knows about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But a Mr. -- A Mr. Djeric, who holds a position in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and I've informed Defence counsel of their response. In principle the Federal Republic sees no problem, but they need to take a government decision, which cannot be taken until the government meets, which will -- and he estimates that it would be on Thursday that we would get the response. But I need to tell Your Honours that because clearly Your Honours could make such orders as you wished if -- and if the Federal Republic was not content, then we couldn't carry -- Your Honours couldn't carry them out. Your Honour asks how would the public perception change. Your Honour, if the man -- if the accused is given provisional release, he is effectively a free man to do as he wishes subject to the restrictions on movement that Your Honours may apply. Your Honour, he's a free man at a time when a trial charging him with genocide and other major breaches of international humanitarian law is well underway and evidence has been called, we would submit, that shows his involvement in those crimes. The general public, those in Bosnia, in the former territories of what was then Yugoslavia, who were the victims of these crimes would not understand, we submit, why a man was not being kept under arrest at a time when he should be being tried, his medical condition notwithstanding. Now, the terms on which the Prosecutor would agree to, as it were, a transfer out of the jurisdiction of this Court are those which effectively mean not only is this man still under detention of a sort, even though it's in a place where he can receive medical treatment, but the terms are such that should the time come that he is fit to attend trial and fit to remain in the detention unit here, then he will be brought back to this Court and the trial will be completed. Now, Your Honour, those are what we consider -- we may be wrong, but we think not. As an office, this office has dealt with the victims of crimes for now a considerable number of years, and we do submit that those who were the victims in this case -- and may I make it absolutely clear that each of the cases which the -- or many of the cases, I should say, which this office prosecutes have different victims from different ethnicities. In this particular case, it happens to be the Muslims -- the Muslim population and the Croat population of Bosnia. In other cases it has been Serbs; in other cases it has been Croats, and so on and so forth. But it is our submission that the public is entitled to know that people charged with these offences are not effectively, because of the state of health, however sympathetic one is to a man in this position, but because of his state of health is effectively not being given carte blanche to walk the streets of either Banja Luka or Belgrade. Now, this is particularly important in respect of Banja Luka. Your Honour, this trial in any showing will be an ongoing trial, whether it goes on at the moment against General Talic or only against Mr. Brdjanin, is a matter which Your Honours will have to decide upon when we've dealt with this. But the presence, for example, of General Talic walking the streets - because as Your Honour says, quite rightly, the hospital treatment may not take up the whole time - is not conducive to the persuasion for witnesses to attend this court and give evidence. The perception -- Your Honour once asked me about -- in relation to protective measures for witnesses that -- what the particular area was like in terms of threat. And the difficulty is it may objectively not be a high threat risk to somebody testifying, but subjectively to the person who's going to testify the presence of other ethnicities is a problem. It does cause fear and does make it less likely for witnesses to attend. So therefore, Your Honours, our submission on this is that effectively we are seeking to assist in the humanitarian aid to General Talic -- in other words, that should he be enabled to receive that treatment in his own country so that he can be dealt with in a language that he understands. We could have - and Your Honour, I make this absolutely clear - we could have objected and said, "No, there's more than adequate -- in fact, as we heard the other the day, top specialists working in this country. It is our application that he should remain within the confines of the Netherlands, have such treatment as was suggested by one of the doctors as an outpatient, and be returned to the detention unit." But we do have sympathy for the plight that General Talic now finds himself in, and so we are now prepared to say that he should be allowed to return to Yugoslavia but under terms that will mean that should he recover sufficiently to be enabled for his trial to continue at that stage, he will be returned. So Your Honour, I hope that deals with the matters that Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I take it, you had two options: keeping him here in the detention unit receiving hospitalisation treatment or whatever is required, but remaining in detention here at the detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same picture, same story but back in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you opted for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We opted for that because, as I say, we have sympathy for the plight that the general finds himself in. But at the same time we have to look at our duty to those whom we represent in all these trials, and that is the victims of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, could you enlighten this Chamber on the position of -- your position with regard to Ms. Korner's -- or the Prosecution's proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Gladly, Your Honours. First of all, it is the -- it is our -- if we understood correctly the OTP, it appears that the Office of the Prosecutor is having a wrong perception of what we are asking by this motion. What we are asking by this motion is not that the General Talic would be freed altogether but would be provisionally released. According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, it is understandable that the accused is released -- provisionally released under very strict conditions and the conditions which the Trial Chamber deems appropriate from -- from case to case. So it does go without saying, if I may say so, that the -- that the accused is expected to be brought to the Tribunal on the order of the same Trial Chamber that provisionally released him. That is why the guarantees are usually taken in this Tribunal for the accused. As to the -- as to the response, Your Honours, with all due respect the Defence of General Talic does consider this response a yes-and-no response. First of all, the Prosecutor -- the Prosecution is on one hand opposing the motion for provisional release and at the same time declares to be in favour of the treatment of the accused to be conducted in a military medical academy in Belgrade. The motion for provisional release was filed mainly and only because of the medical -- status of medical health of our client. That was the reason behind why the motion for provisional release at this time was filed. So it is our understanding that the Prosecution is not opposing the fact, which it even clearly states in the response, that it doesn't oppose the fact that General Talic is very seriously ill and that he does require therapy and medical treatment. The only thing which in fact the Prosecution is opposing are the conditions of this -- of this provisional release. It is therefore our -- our position is that the Rule 54 cannot be applicable in this case. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal in the previous cases and more -- and even in one almost similar case of General Djukic has been very clear that the provisions of Rule 65 has been and in fact has been -- has been applied. And General Djukic was provisionally released on humanitarian basis only because of the nature of his serious illness. The Prosecution response has quite a bit of factual things which I would not like to bother the Trial Chamber at this time because the Trial Chamber heard the testimony of the witnesses and therefore can decide what is -- what the witnesses really said before this Trial Chamber. But I would like to comment on two things: The Prosecution response and Your Honours -- Your Honour have just read that -- and commenting on the public interest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One -- let me interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think at this point in time we can admit the representative of the FRY, because we will obviously need to ask him some questions, and we will also need to hear what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, Mr. Zecevic, until he comes in, because more or less I can anticipate what you're going to deal with now and I think he -- it's better if --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's better if he is in the courtroom to hear what you have to say. Basically what I would like you to address, both of you, is the reality of the situation, and the reality of the situation, point number one, is that General Talic may or may not be today fit or unfit to stand trial or to remain at the detention centre. That is very important to start with. But what is more important is what we referred to towards the end of the last sitting that we had, the last hearing. And precisely, if General Talic were to be kept here in The Hague, would it be possible -- would it be compatible with his fundamental rights, those applicable and relevant fundamental rights to keep him in the detention, proceed with the trial, and give him all the medical attention that he requires within the medical prognosis scenario that we were given by the three doctors. The detention medical unit officer, and the two consultants -- the two experts that we heard. Combine everything together, and more or less you have a pretty clear scenario, although it varies to some degree and in certain details. The reality of the situation is that I am informed, at least, that there is no way you can keep one of the detainees here in The Hague and guarantee a medical treatment and hospitalisation, if necessary, for a long period of time. That is out of the questions. I have checked up on it, and I have been told that there is an agreement -- an informed agreement, not even a written agreement, between the Tribunal and the Dutch authorities, ensuring that any detainee who requires treatment will receive it. But we're talking on a short-haul affair and not something that can go on indefinitely. That has not been specifically addressed so far between the two -- between the Tribunal and the Dutch government. And I think we -- we have to call a spade a spade and this is where we have to start from. The situation may be tenable, may be one which we could deal with now, without any major problems, without any major aggravation and without in any way prejudicing or harming the rights of General Talic, but today is today and tomorrow things may change. And if things change tomorrow, the situation may become untenable. Now, it's true what the Prosecution says in its motion -- in your motion that the situation is not very clear. You don't know what to expect. The situation can remain status quo, as it is now, for -- for months, or it could change and deteriorate very rapidly. And I think I see a lot of wisdom in the approach that the Prosecution has taken in not adopting a radical opposition to your request for provisional release. I think it is something that we have to acknowledge, that the Prosecution has -- does realise the different combinations and permutations that are involved apart from the humanitarian aspect. The only other problem that I see is -- is the following: The Rules do authorise this Tribunal to detain an accused person either in the facilities here in The Hague or facilities offered by another country or available in another country. In fact, it says that "In exceptional circumstances, the accused may be held in facilities outside of the host country." So the request that the Prosecution is making -- or the proposition -- sorry if I am using the word "request" -- the proposition of the Prosecution definitely is one which is contemplated which falls under the general umbrella of the Rule that I have just been reading from. What I want from you, Mr. Zecevic, is more or less an answer to the same question that I posed to the Prosecution: What difference do you see between an order providing for the provisional release of your client accompanied with facilitating all that is required or may become necessary for his medical treatment and with the usual guarantees and an order along the lines being proposed by the Prosecution which will give him the opportunity to be in his own country, to be with his family, to receive all the necessary treatment, and which would also offer the guarantees that we would normally require, in the case of a provisional release in case his return to this Tribunal, is necessitated. What difference do you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that would be the case, I would -- it is my assumption that Your Honours do not see any difference and neither do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't say that. I asked -- I put the question to Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wanting to know why she opted for one, rather than the other. And I'm putting the same question to you: Why you are opposing Ms. Korner's proposition and standing by your request?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honours, we are -- we filed the motion for provisional released base on Rule 65, which we think is the only rule which does deal with the -- with the actual provisional release. What Your Honours have just read is -- is Rule 64, if I -- if I correctly know the Rules, but -- and I believe I do. And the motion, the motion of the Prosecutor, was not filed under Rule 64 or not -- or the Rule 64 was invoked, but Rule 54 was invoked in this particular -- in this particular case. Why we are opposing is that from the Prosecutor's response, we cannot see the actual -- the actual way how the Prosecutor does think this is achievable at all, because it involves so many different authorities that has to be consulted with and it, be all means, takes time, and the time is the only thing, as I emphasised so many times -- the time is the only thing that we don't have unfortunately, because of the serious situation of the medical health of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is not correct, because if your client requires treatment here in The Hague, which he have it within the minute, within the hour, any treatment. And I don't think the treatment in this country will be any less than the treatment he would receive in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But Your Honours stated yourself that it has been brought to our attention that the treatment cannot be conducted within the premises of the UNDU and if the treatment would start now, then the treatment will have to finish here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. There are two kinds of interventions that he can be subjected to. One is the intervention which would glue his pleura to the thorax. That is a simple intervention which is almost ambulatory. I mean, it's -- he will go in the morning and come out of the hospital the same day. And the other one is chemotherapy, and that can be started straight away and can be continued in Belgrade or in -- wherever later on, without any prejudice to his health, ensuring that he will be able to travel when the doctors will certify that there is absolutely no danger for him to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I'm referring to is not a medical treatment in the detention unit but medical treatment in a proper hospital here in The Hague, which I can more or less guarantee to you, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, the first intervention that you mentioned is just to help General Talic's condition that -- that the fluid does not happen in this enormous quantity as it does in his lungs. And the actual -- the only treatment which is -- which was suggested by the doctors is the chemotherapy, actually. If I have correctly understood the chief medical officer of the UNDU and the warden of the UNDU, they have -- they have expressed their gravest reserves about the possibility of the treatment be conducted in the hospital of -- in Netherlands because of the security reasons, because of the reluctance of the hospital to accept such a patient and so on. But in any case, I would not like to go into an area which -- which is not my -- my area, so to speak, because it is appropriate for the medical staff or medical doctors to address to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've still not answered my question. Granted for the time being --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that what you have just said so far, based on what others have said, is correct, 100 per cent, namely that there is no way that you can more or less guarantee General Talic his rights, plus medical treatment, plus everything here in The Hague in the present conditions -- given also what we have been told by the consultants at least and also by the medical doctor that a few days here and a few days here are not going to make a difference at all for the time being, because the situation has not deteriorated to the extent where we have to act within the hour -- why should the only option open to us, available, be that of provisional release to the exclusion of the option that is being proposed or offered by the Prosecution? This is what I would like you to convince us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have based, as I said just prior to this -- we have based our motion on the Rule 65, which gives a possibility of provisional release to be granted to the accused. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal has recognised only this rule for the provisional release of the accused, so as to speak, Rule 65. There has never been a case, to my knowledge, whether other rule, such as 52, has been -- has been used for these purposes. That is why we have based our submission on the 65, and we don't -- what I am about to address is that we don't really see the difference between the 65 -- the difference between our motion and the actual standing of the Prosecutor, because the Prosecutor is actually and only addressing to the conditions of the provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're saying that to all effects and purposes, except of law, what the Prosecution is proposing is a provisional release, which, however, is not a provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly our opinion. That is why I said this is a yes-and-no response, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you're maintaining that it's sort of a save-face proposition on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggest anything, Your Honours. I'm just giving my opinion on the response which I received, as you know, two hours before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's why I asked you whether you wanted more time --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I am perfectly capable to give submissions on that, if you allow me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Earlier I wanted to give two comments on this response filed by the Prosecutor. The first comment is about the issue of the public perception. The Defence is wondering whether the public -- their interest and the perception even of the Office of the Prosecutor is that the -- this, the same office, is bound by the provisions of international convent of civil and political rights and European convention of protection of human rights and fundamental freedom. Ms. Korner was just -- was just addressing the issue where our client has been charged with very serious crimes. At the same time before this Tribunal, Ms. Plavsic was charged with genocide and released, and in fact now is on provisional release, and that -- and it did not destroy the public perception of the Prosecution at all. That is why in such a case where we have a very serious situation, medical situation, we really cannot give credit for the -- for the statement that the public perception would in any way be inflicted by the provisional release of our client. Also, the Prosecutor in its response is claiming that there is a prima facie responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget that. Jump to the next submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand, Your Honours, that was exactly my opinion as well. Your Honours, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal has been cited in our motion for provisional release, and that is the most similar case is that of General Djukic from back in 1996. The Trial Chamber in that decision from 24th of April, 1996 found that "the accused Djukic suffered from the incurable disease and that it is in the terminal phase. Further, the Trial Chamber found that the very serious state of medical health of General Djukic is incompatible with any kind of detention and that the palliative care which is necessary requires a different environment." Ultimately, the Trial Chamber decided and granted the motion for provisional release for humanitarian reasons only and authorised his immediate return from Netherlands to that the accused could rejoin his family. This decision, in our opinion, is in complete accordance with the numerous provisions of international humanitarian law, such as the basis principles for the treatment of prisoners, standard minimum rules for treatment of prisoners, universal convention of humanitarian rights, American, European, and African convention and ultimately the Rules of ICTY from 1999. In the Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic, Alagic and Kubura, the Trial Chamber II granted provisional release on 19th of December, 2001 and reasoned "That Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence must be read in the light of the international convention on civil and political rights and European convention for the protection of humanitarian rights and fundamental freedoms." Further, the Trial Chamber held that "It must interpret Rule 65 with regard to the factual basis of a single case and with respect to the concrete situation of the individual human being and not in abstracto. Further the Trial Chamber stressed that the procedural measures should not be capricious or obsessive and that if it's sufficient to use more lenient measure, it must be applied. The position of the Defence is that the Rule 65 gives the opportunity to the Trial Chamber to order provisional release of the accused based on two basic requirements: The requirements in short - I will not bother the Trial Chamber with that - is that the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the accused will reappear on the request of the Trial Chamber and second, that the accused does not pose danger to victims, witnesses, or any third person. Also, the opportunity to be heard is given to the host country and state which the accused seeks to be released. The host country already informed this Trial Chamber that it doesn't oppose the release, so as well Republika Srpska has already filed a guarantee with the Tribunal in form, recognised the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and the representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is here with us now and will testify in -- concerning the readiness of FRY to issue and fulfil the guarantee and accordingly ensure the Trial Chamber that the accused will reappear on request of the Trial Chamber. As for the victims and witnesses, the Defence points out that the witnesses and victims from the municipality of Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please show down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you are creating difficulties for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that the Defence acknowledge no witness or victims are residing in Belgrade, Yugoslavia. Moreover the state of health of our client does not in any way permit him to engage in anything but the therapy and medical treatment of his illness at this moment. The Rule 65 does give the Trial Chamber a power to impose any condition it may deem appropriate for the case. So in this respect, the -- the Defence, being seized by the -- by the urgency and the need of our client to undergo therapy as soon as practically possible, does not have any suggestion as to which conditions should be or should not be imposed. And therefore, we will accept any condition within, of course, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and which would -- which would ensure that our client does get what we are seeking to have. Your Honours, in this particular case we have heard experts -- three experts, one of them being a chief medical officer of the UNDU, and two other leading specialists, oncologists, who were summoned and appeared before this Trial Chamber to verify the diagnosis of the medical officer of UNDU, which they eventually did. Both oncologists concluded after reviewing the medical records, and one of them performing physical examination and biopsy and subsequently received the results from the tissue that the nature of illness is serious and that it is inoperable and incurable and that the health of our client will deteriorate rather fast. They both also suggested chemotherapy as the only medical treatment which might prolong the life of the accused. The warden informed the Trial Chamber of the impossibility of ensuring the chemotherapy treatment or proper medical care within the UNDU and Dutch hospital may not be a solution because of the security reasons. The chief medical officer of the UNDU within the scope of his duty and responsibilities, in accordance with the Rule 33 of the Rules of Detention of this Tribunal, declared the accused unfit for trial and not fit to remain in detention. His fitness was basically the issue that the medical officer and the two specialists disagreed upon. But with all due respect to the specialist oncologists, they can be, and are experts for diagnosis of the illness and not for the detention and whether a person is fit to remain in detention or fit to stand trial, because as one of them pointed out rightly, none of his patients under treatment does come from any kind of detention facility. So their knowledge in this respect is rather limited, contrary to that of the chief medical officer of the UNDU. Whether the accused can stand trial for another week does not seem to be in our minds at all important, given the fact that according to what we know at this point, it would be about all that he can stand. It doesn't change anything with respect to the dynamics of this trial, but significantly reduces the changes of immediate therapy and possible prolongation of life for a couple of months, to which any human being must be entitled. There is no doubt, Your Honours, that our client has to start therapy immediately. The right to adequate medical care is one of the fundamental human rights and our client has been deprived of his fundamental human right. Eight days has already lapsed since we became aware of the medical condition of our client, and every additional day directly diminishes the chance of any positive effect of the therapy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The overall condition of -- I will, sorry. And not only that, but his overall condition at this moment leaves the option of different possible therapies to choose, since undoubtedly his health will deteriorate, the options will be fewer and fewer. The Prosecution, as stated in their response, is satisfied that General Talic is suffering from inoperable and incurable disease. Also, the Prosecution recognises the problems with the treatment therapy to be administered while in custody here at the UNDU. And so in fact the Prosecution recognises the relevant facts to the decision of this Tribunal concerning our motion for provisional release, yet it still opposes the motion. The Defence from the -- from the old stated reasons just right now, in the reasons stated in our motion, respectfully request that the motion for provisional release be granted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I give the floor again to Ms. Korner, may I just rebut the suggestion that you have made that by postponing or adjourning the hearing for today, this Chamber has violated the rights -- the fundamental rights of your client. May I refer to the last statement made by the medical officer of the detention unit when faced with a direct question "Would another week, would a few days, even more than another week of this -- General Talic staying in detention in any way harm his health?" The answer was, " No." This was the same person who had stated categorically in a medical certificate that he was unfit to remain in the detention unit. And may I also remind you, sir, that the -- one of the experts that were brought here, and this Trial Chamber even suggested that we should tell General Talic to go and play tennis. This is how far we have prejudiced General Talic's health. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not in any way say that this Trial Chamber has violated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can -- we can check -- go straight --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can go straight to the part --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said that for eight days he has been deprived of his fundamental right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- there are just two matters that I want to come back on that were said, leaving aside the question of Dr. Dr. Valke, as opposed to the two eminent specialists, that is Your Honour heard from. The first is this: Effectively what Mr. Zecevic is arguing is that because this kind of application has not been dealt with before, other than under Rule 65, it's therefore contrary to the Rules. Your Honours have in fact drawn our attention to Rule 64, which regrettably we failed to mention in the motion, but in any event it's absolutely clear that Your Honours have power to make such orders as Your Honours think fit. And the whole point is the Prosecution is opposing provisional release under Rule 65. What it's asking for is an order for the remand of General Talic at a place outside the detention unit in The Hague. Your Honours, I don't know what -- whether the quoting from the authorities has been selective or not. I don't know whether Your Honours were provided with a list of authorities. We weren't. I can say that in respect of General Djukic, the situation was very different. General Djukic had been charged on an indictment. General Djukic -- the trial had not started. I -- can I put it this way: I'm disappointed that Your Honours do not consider the fact that evidence has been called, we would submit, implicating General Talic in offences, unrebutted but raising a prima facie case for him is irrelevant. Because that's one of the major differences. No evidence had been called in General Djukic's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's both ways. It cuts both ways. Because if you are correct, then you don't have to worry much -- or at least as much as you would have had to worry had the trial not even started as yet. If it is -- if you are correct in your submission that this is an ongoing trial, in the course of which prima facie evidence has already been provided, to pin General Talic against the indictment, then you should worry less than if the trial were just about to start tomorrow and we are releasing General Talic before you present your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid that -- Your Honour, it may be that it's -- I'm not quite following that. The reason that we've -- I've raised -- we've raised this is because it's a case where the general public has heard evidence -- and General Talic has heard evidence. And in the event -- and this is one of the real difficulties, as we discussed last week, the prognosis is uncertain now, it may be that chemotherapy can alleviate General Talic's symptoms to such an extent that he is able to resume the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also -- I'm sorry to rebut in again like this, but you also have the last document that was presented to us by Dr. Baas, namely that his final prognosis is that General Talic won't make it beyond -- beyond a year. That's his final prognosis. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We all know that this trial will not be in a year's time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was a slight -- it is possible theoretically, of course -- depending on -- there are a number of available options still to discuss -- to conclude this trial against General Talic within a couple of months by radically cutting down the evidence that we intended to call, theoretically. All of that is possible. And of course I know what Dr. Baas said. But as against that, he said the percentage of people surviving longer is smaller, but the other doctor, Dr. Van --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Meerbeek.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- said that 40 per cent of people survive two years long. That's the real difficulty. But Your Honour what we're saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's certain is the situation will not become any better as we go along, but it become definitely worse. It will deteriorate. And there will come a point in time, for sure, irrespective of what we will decide now -- but given the course, the normal course of expectations in such a disease, where definitely there will be no options but one. So should we wait until that moment, or should we apply the humanitarian basis rule that was applied in Djukic, given that in Djukic the situation was far advanced, more advanced that it is now, because if you read Djukic well, most important -- there are two basic points made in that judgement. One is that the decision is reached solely on humanitarian grounds; and secondly, that that person was unfit at that time to stand trial. We have declaration by two experts that that person at the present moment is fit to stand trial, but also that the situation will get worse. So this is what I would like you to address at -- whenever it's convenient to you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, I'm addressing this. But Your Honour, all this -- that's the real major problem. The situation will get worse eventually. I mean, effectively as I think somebody said -- Dr. Valke said, General Talic has effectively received a sentence of death. But the question is: How long? Now, Your Honour, the problem with all of this is that General Talic can receive treatment. That treatment, the chemotherapy, may give him extra time to live. That time that he has to live is uncertain. It could be anything theoretically up to five years. Your Honour, in those circumstances the Prosecution are saying, in terms we have started a trial against this man of genocide. This man -- we say, we submit, that is our case, is guilty of genocide and we are in the process of calling evidence to show that. We understand the situation as it now stands. He is -- okay, temporarily he may be fit but he needs treatment and we accept that. But we are saying, fine, he receives that treatment but still in detention. If the prognosis gets no better, his health does not increase, and we will know that from medical treatment, very well. That's one matter. But if it does, then we say it is proper and fit that this man should be tried for those crimes. It is not right that the deaths of thousands of people should be allowed to go, as it were, untried, unaired, and that is the reason, Your Honour. We're here to represent the interests of the victims, of justice. This is what the mandate of this Tribunal is. Now, having said all that, Your Honour, what we are now saying at this stage in time: We don't know what's going to happen. What we do know is that at present he needs treatment. We are prepared on behalf of the Prosecution to accede to the request that it be treatment given to him in his own country, taking the former Yugoslavia now as a whole, because we would certainly submit that Banja Luka is thoroughly inappropriate for him to be going back to. And we are prepared that that treatment should be given to him in a Belgrade hospital subject to the consent of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So my last -- one moment, Madam Fauveau. I will come back to you very soon. I'll face you with a very direct question. I fully understand your preoccupation with the public perception, particularly with regard to victims and witnesses. I don't want you to misunderstand me or to even think for a moment that that is your concern but it's not our concern. It is definitely our concern as well. What I would like you to explain to me is this, how victims and witnesses related to this particular case and other cases that may be pending before this Tribunal and which may come to this Tribunal later on, will be happier if they knew that General Talic, instead of being guarded in a detention unit here in The Hague by UN guards and supervised by a UN commandant is being held in a military hospital in Belgrade supervised by, I suppose, someone from Belgrade and guarded by, I suppose, someone from Belgrade. Do you honestly believe that victims and witnesses will feel more at ease with such a situation rather than if they knew that he is on provisional release with whoever has an interest to keep an open eye, to make sure that the conditions are being fulfilled, are indeed being fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we didn't feel that, we wouldn't have done this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you feel --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We would have -- we would have agreed to provisional release other than obviously, as I say, Banja Luka being thoroughly inappropriate, but the terms of provisional release to Belgrade. It is our belief as an office -- and may I say this -- as Your Honours know, is part of the reason we asked for the adjournment was so we could discuss it with the Prosecutor herself. It is the belief of the Prosecutor herself that this does make a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I shall refrain from repeating anything that my colleague has already said. But there is something, on the other hand, which I would like to add. It is true that it's a week today -- it's exactly a week that the two experts have said that General Talic may perhaps be capable of standing trial. One of them said for one week and the other one said "certainly for one week," and "for two weeks it was questionable." At this very point in time we have no certainty that General Talic is capable of coming here to stand trial, but we are certain that he is not capable, because the doctor of the detention unit said that General Talic was not fit to stand trial. It is true that he said that he may remain in the detention unit for another couple of days, but that's not the same thing. To be in the detention unit and to stand trial here, standing trial meaning having all the mental capacity to be able to follow the proceedings and to be able to participate in his defence. I think there are two things in this case that are important: The first is that General Talic should receive, as quickly as possible, the appropriate medical treatment. And I will not dwell on this, because my colleague has already covered that issue at length. I would also say that the problem regarding his ability to stand trial is linked to his being in the detention unit, because after all what is the aim of detention? The only aim is to ensure the presence of the accused at trial, and he is not capable of attending. Why detain him, then? That is the question I am addressing to Madam Korner and also to you. What is the purpose of detention in this situation when one is sure that he will not see the end of these proceedings, he will not be there to witness them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I'm being -- the answer, we're not seeking to detain him at the detention unit, but we're seeking to ensure that until such time as there is a clearer picture of what the situation is, he is in detention, even though that detention be in a hospital in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, for the time being -- and Mr. Ackerman, I haven't asked you whether you have any submissions. I suppose you don't. Sir, I'm addressing you now. The Chamber would like to thank you, first of all, for taking an interest and also for coming over to assist these -- this particular debate also because General Talic is seeking permission from this Tribunal, apart from to be provisionally released but also to receive treatment -- medical treatment in your country, in Belgrade particularly. And therefore, according to the Rules we also must hear what you have to say. Your government has provided us with a -- what I would call a provisionally letter of intent -- provisional letter of intent of guarantees, which I am sure you are aware of. And just for the record, it is a letter of intent which is not conclusive but which, in more than one way, lets -- puts the Tribunal, the Chamber in a position which it could expect a full document containing the guarantees that we would normally require from the country where the accused is returned to. To put you into the picture, because I'm not quite sure whether you are aware of the entire picture: The latest -- or the most recent development in the request that has been made by motion by General Talic for his provisional release is that the Prosecutor is opposing the provisional release, as we understand it, in law, but is proposing as an alternative that General Talic will be flown to the military hospital in Belgrade and -- where he will receive medical treatment, all the medical treatment that that hospital can offer him and which he would like to receive, and that for all intensive purposes of law, particularly the Rules governing this Tribunal which relate to detention on remand, the authorities in Belgrade step into the shoes effectively, of the detention unit here in The Hague, the detention unit of this Tribunal, the United Nations Detention Unit, and take it upon themselves to detain -- not only to cure, but only to detain as long as necessary General Talic in the military hospital, providing the usual service of detention; in other words, supervision and guards. This apart from the normal, usual guarantees that we would request from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or from Republika Srpska or from Bosnia and Herzegovina, whichever, which more or less are the same guarantees that one would have in -- in provisional release. But there is something also beyond these guarantees, and that is the Prosecution -- were you aware of this -- of all, this by the way?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, distinguished member of the Court. Let me introduce myself in the beginning. My name is Slavoljub Caric and I am the counsellor of the embassy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may remain seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I am an official representative of FRY in this case, in this hearing. Thank you for your compliments to our government and thank you for your presentation of developments in this case. I am aware of the letter of Mr. Sarkic, Deputy Minister of Justice of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and so I can only add something as explanation. Let me read that in Serbian language. [Interpretation] Your Honours, in connection with the request of the accused for provisional release, allow me to inform you that the Federal Ministry of Justice of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has proposed to the federal government that it issue guarantees for the provisional release of General Talic. Practice shows that in all previous cases, the federal government has adopted such suggestions for technical reasons and the absence of a large number of ministers and member of the government, the federal government was not in a position to hold its regular session and to pass a formal decision on this matter. We expect the federal government to review the issue and make a decision at its first next session, which has been scheduled for Thursday, the 19th of September, 2002. I should like to underline that in previous cases when this Tribunal issued a ruling on the provisional release of the accused, such as Biljana Plavsic, Miodrag Jokic, and Momcilo Gruban, the competent Yugoslav authorities were prepared to take upon themselves the following obligations: To take over the accused from the Dutch authorities at Schiphol airport, on a date and time determined by the Tribunal and to escort him on his journey to Yugoslavia; to escort the accused from Belgrade to Schiphol airport and to surrender him to the Dutch authorities at a time determined by the Tribunal; the accused will report to the police station on a daily basis and the Tribunal will be informed about this in writing, including any absence -- possible absence of the accused if this should occur; also, immediately inform the Tribunal should the accused make an attempt to escape. Your Honours, that would be as much as I have to say at this point in time, following the instructions given to me by my government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. I will continue with giving you more details as to the counterproposition or the proposition of the Prosecution, because this goes well beyond the usual guarantees --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think this gentleman can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think he needs to be informed. And what I was going to suggest is that we give him a copy of your response which he will transmit to capitol and then he should be in a position to inform us, because we need to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no way we can proceed on your proposition --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Absolutely, Your Honour. But I think as I said, there have been direct dealings with a gentleman named Mr. Djeric -- which I think this gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the gentleman who sent us the letter on behalf of the Yugoslav government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right -- I thought it was Djeric. But he gave us the information already that this gentleman has just passed on to you, namely that until the government meets on Thursday morning, there can be no decision one way or the other. And he has all the -- the conditions, which are listed in our response, are those that we've transmitted with the request to know whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be able to fulfil those conditions. So that's -- that's the situation, Your Honour, rather than -- but certainly we can give him a copy of the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we ought to proceed along those lines. What I suggest we do: It's quarter to 4.00 now. I propose to have a break, because I think we have give the interpreters a very hard time this last hour and a half. We will resume in 30 minutes. In the meantime, Madam Registrar, I entrust you with giving a copy of the Prosecution's response to the councillor of the embassy. And please have a look at it, because basically we would require to know, when possible, specific -- I mean, a specific response -- the specific response to the -- of your government to the conditions attached to the proposition of the Prosecution, independent of the guarantees that are normally attached to a normal, ordinary provisional release order. Okay? The two are different. Some elements are common to both; some elements are pertinent only to what is being proposed by the Prosecution. And we would obviously need to know, because you -- a decision would obviously be based on the information that will be forthcoming, apart from other issues. We will resume in 30 minutes' time. I thank you. And as soon as you -- we resume, the gentleman will be brought in the courtroom again. Mr. Brdjanin, if he wants to remain here -- you are free to remain. If you would like to go back to the detention unit, you're free to go there. I mean, it's -- it's up to you. All right? Discuss it with your lawyer, and -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, the representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just -- I double-checked on the name of the gentleman, and as I thought, it is in fact a Vladimir Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: D-j-e-r-i-c, with whom the Office of the Prosecutor has been dealing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You spoke with -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he's the adviser to the Federal Minister for Foreign Affairs and president to the National Council for cooperation with the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's good to know. So as I was trying to explain to you, the purpose for handing you the -- that particular document, that is, the Prosecution's response to the motion for provisional release, was not to, in any way, procure any kind of comment from you. Certainly not. It's just to let you have the document which would spare me having to explain one point after the other to you, for eventual transmission by your embassy to your capitol. So you have the document, and more or less now on the basis of that document you know what to transmit to your government in Belgrade. So basically, sir, at the end of the day when the Yugoslav government would have had opportunity to meet what -- and decide, what we would require, is a decision that would cover the two possibilities; in other words, the possibility of a transfer to Belgrade under the terms and conditions outlined by the Prosecution in their response, in other words, for all intents and purposes one of detention under the Rules of this Tribunal but effectively administered by the authorities in Belgrade. Alternatively, the usual conditions that are attached to a provisional release, with which your government is familiar, because as you explained earlier on, there have been instances in the past where provisional release was ordered -- granted by this Tribunal against the guarantees or with the guarantees of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So that is the position. If you have further comments, of course, you are free to -- to make them. I would invite you to -- if not, I would invite you to remain seated to follow the rest of the debate until it is of interest to you. Should you like, at any moment, to leave because the debate turns into matters that are of no further interest to you, then obviously you just ask me and you would be able to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your explanation and for obtaining me with provisional response to motion for provisional release of General Talic. I would like to clarify something. I have strictly instructions of my government to propose conditions, as I explained during my speech. That's the same what Mr. Djeric promised. Mr. Djeric is a council of Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It is a different person than me, but our attitudes are the same. So nothing more and nothing less of -- yes. And I can only aware [As interpreted] distinguished Trial Chamber and you, Your Honour, that the competent Yugoslav authorities will consider all proposed conditions very precisely and carefully from top to bottom, and as soon as possible let you know what is acceptable for our side. Obviously the government of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia bear in mind urgency and all the aspects of this case because I consider myself, it requires no minute [As interpreted] of sifting complicated facts. Thank you for your understanding and attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Now, I think this first part of the debate we can consider to be concluded. Are there any further submissions that you'd like to make with regard to the case proper, because there are three possible decisions that this Chamber could take. One is to turn down, to reject outright, the motion for provisional release. The second is to accept the motion for provisional release. The third is to accept the counterproposal or the proposal of the Prosecution. I see no options, except maybe a fourth option, which could be a combination of both, the last two options that I mentioned. Given any of these three situations -- let's start from situation number one: Outright rejection of the motion for provisional release. I need hardly elaborate on this. In my mind, I see a plethora of consequences that there could be relative to the presence of accused Talic in the courtroom or his absence. That's number one. How -- if this -- the continuation of his detention in the unit is accompanied, as it would definitely be should we reject the motion for provisional release, with medical treatment -- we have already heard the testimony of the three medical doctors that have testified here, and they all agree that -- particularly with regard to chemotherapy there will, even if -- irrespective of the number of cycles that this would undertake, that there is a period during which General Talic would not be able to be present here. And of course the reality of the situation, that the medical condition of General Talic will only get worse and certainly will not get any better. So that is the first one. The second option, should we decide to grant provisional release. Then of course we have a situation whereby General Talic is returned to his country. Usually you would have included according to the case law of this Tribunal, the practice of this Tribunal, one of the conditions that has normally been attached to an order for provisional release is the undertaking by the accused to waive his right to be present while he or she is provisionally released. In this present case you will, of course, realise immediately that the situation is different because we have a person who is suffering from the -- who is in the terminal phase of a serious illness which may, from time to time, bring about a situation whereby he would not be in a position to waive his right to be present in this Tribunal. And this is also another problem that we may have. In other words, I'm making it very clear that any suggestion that General Talic can now, on the 17th of September, 2002, guarantee that he is from now onwards waiving his right to be present, irrevocably and unconditionally, is something that legally this Chamber is not prepared to accept, because the situation may change medically from time to time. And even not medically. It could change from time to time. That's the second option. The third option: If General Talic is returned to Belgrade, where he remains in detention, we still have more or less the same problem that I have just referred to a minute ago, namely his waiver to be present for the hearings -- or for the sittings, but also other considerations that may be relative to his continued presence in this Tribunal. On top of all this, there is the reality of medical picture that we have. We all know that none of the three prognoses that we have had are good. The prognoses are slightly different, but they are bad. So that is bound to have an effect on the future of this trial. And I wonder if in relation to what this Chamber has to decide next -- in the immediate future, you have anything to submit also with regard to all this. I'm sure that you have given this -- these matters a lot of -- a lot of thought, because they are not something that you would not expect. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Your Honour has just expressed a position. Until Your Honour has ruled on that, it's very difficult to say what course we would invite Your Honours to take, because of course we can suggest a course. But if Your Honours were, for example, to reject the -- outright, which is an option that Your Honours have referred to, the request for provisional release or the Prosecution's suggestion of detention elsewhere than the UN Detention Unit, that would be one matter; releasing him would be another; and the Prosecution's solution, a third. So Your Honour, I take it from what Your Honour has said and what we've heard from the gentleman from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, nothing can happen until Thursday, because Your Honour has got no guarantees either one way or the other from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the present moment we don't have guarantees. We have guarantees from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, we've -- as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that is a part of the chain, but not the entire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, Your Honour, may I make it absolutely clear, because I haven't really addressed Your Honour on it -- because in fact, although it was argued in the -- suggested in the motion, it's not been pursued today. We would strongly resist any kind of removal from The Hague that took General Talic to Banja Luka. We haven't gone into the reasons why, but I'm sure that Your Honour would anticipate them. The only, if you like, concession that we're making is that a transfer from the detention unit should be to Belgrade. Now, Your Honour, if Your Honour wants me to address you on that before we go any further, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would if I were you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to send General Talic back to Banja Luka, where there are still witnesses to come, if not in Banja Luka itself, certainly from the surrounding areas, Your Honour, we would suggest would be wholly detrimental to the progress of this trial, which on any showing will be continuing against Mr. Brdjanin. Your Honour is aware because Your Honours had to deal, from time to time, with the problems we've had with witnesses coming to the Court and with the applications that we make for protective measures and indeed having seen quite recently a report as to the situation in the various municipalities, then we would be submitting very strongly that to send General Talic back to Banja Luka with all the freedom of movement that that entails within Banja Luka and elsewhere would be to present a problem to this Tribunal in the hearing of further evidence, and we may add there's no real reason why he should go to Banja Luka other than Belgrade, because the -- the need for this is treatment, and treatment in his own language. His family can visit him -- can stay in Belgrade, for all we know. It's a matter -- I understand it's some four hours' journey from Banja Luka. Your Honour, I had no idea that Your Honours had the slightest intention of releasing him back to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't ruled out any option.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in that case, we do -- we would strongly urge Your Honours not to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you see, if you read -- I'm sure you have, but the motion for provisional release refers to Belgrade military hospital, as I understand it, as something that may be and will be needed by General Talic and which he -- and that's because he -- his preference for medical treatment is precisely the military medical academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I read Your Honour -- I hadn't appreciated, Your Honour, that -- Your Honour, there was the slightest reason for releasing him to Banja Luka. "The defendant shall remain within the confines of the municipality of Banja Luka except for occasional visits for tests, medical treatment, and therapy, as may be required by the medical doctors to the military medical academy in Belgrade, which is the only specialised institution in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to cope with illnesses of this kind and the place where the defendant can receive the satisfactory medical care." Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution's concession is made on the basis of the need for treatment and not for any other reason at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why in the very beginning of today's sitting, because I had this in the back of my mind all the time -- this is why I stated categorically that for a moment it was difficult for me to envisage a situation whereby General Talic is admitted to the military hospital in Belgrade to receive treatment and remains there for weeks and months on end, because this -- people like him, in his same condition, will go for hospital for one hour, two hours, three hours, and go back home. And then it's only at the very end that they are hospitalised, given morphine or whatever, and given all the palliative treatment that is required at the very end, at the very terminal stages of the disease that's when hospitalisation is continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
