utterances.text: Well, Your Honour didn't make it clear, may I say with respect that you had this paragraph in the back of your mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- I have everything in the back of my mind, because this is the very first paragraph contained in -- in the conclusive part of the motion for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can I not have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But can I make this clear: Your Honour asked about that, but actually asked why the Prosecution -- what the public perception had to do with it. Your Honour didn't actually -- Your Honour mentioned in passing this, and then asked me about the public perception -- sorry, perception. And that's what I was dealing with. But Your Honour, Your Honour will see that what we're saying is -- the hospital. But if the hospital can't keep him or he's not going to be -- then there should be some kind of house arrest in Belgrade. In other words, we're talking about detention. And I believe that this is not just a hospital. There's also a military academy attached, though I'm not a hundred per cent certain. But Your Honour, certainly -- to allow -- we would resist strongly and do resist strongly that he be allowed to go back to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how does that fit in the whole humanitarian discourse? If General Talic -- if the doctors were to come here today and go a step further, beyond what they told us last week, say his condition has deteriorated considerably. We did not anticipate this, but it has happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then Your Honour, the simple answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How -- how would you expect us to deal with General Talic any different than how -- than what this -- the Tribunal decided in the Djukic case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the simple answer: If that happens, then an application can be made to Your Honours to rescind, revoke, vary the terms of the order in some way. But at the moment, Your Honour, that's the whole point. That's why we've taken this position. Nothing is clear. And in general -- may I repeat, Your Honour, General Djukic was an entirely different situation, as indeed are all the other cases where -- which were mentioned for provisional release only; that is, Gruban, Plavsic, the rest. No trial has begun in those cases. This is a very different situation. A trial began in January of this year. But Your Honour, if the situation deteriorates, it will take 24 hours to have an application made to Your Honours for a variation in the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he goes to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- that's a different matter. We would have to hear what the terms are. But Your Honour, we're not talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But would you object --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- To his return to Banja Luka at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I cannot say, and nor at this stage should Your Honours with respect be considering it. What will be the situation if his condition suddenly deteriorates? We're talking about what is the situation now. And the situation now that this man has incurable cancer. But the length of time that he will live is uncertain. The condition of this man at the moment is contrary to what Dr. Valke told Your Honours. Good. He is apparently in pretty good physical condition. He is able, in fact, to remain in detention at the moment. He is fit to stand trial. But we do not wish to stand in his way -- humanitarian way that he should receive treatment that will prolong his life. And this is -- but this is what we're dealing with at the moment. Nothing else, Your Honours. Not what if; not what may; but what is the situation today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It goes beyond that. Because you have the reality of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we had the uncertainty of a situation, we could -- we were talking of possible years to come until the situation really crystallizes, then I would -- I would understand what you're saying. But in spite of the few uncertainties that have been highlighted, there is a big certainty and that is that you have cancer, you have a metastasis. For the time being it's limited to where it is limited. It is incurable. It is inoperable. And chemotherapy can lengthen or prolong life by maybe three months. This is -- this is the prognosis that we had. So it's not going to cure the patient, but it's going to prolong -- if it does, because people respond differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, is making the point that I'm trying to make at this stage. Your Honour is dealing with today and now, not what is going to happen in the future. Your Honour, at the moment the urgent thing is -- and I accept entirely what's been said on his behalf -- that he begin such course of treatment that he's prepared to undertake. We do not know actually whether or not General Talic wishes to undertake chemotherapy. That's entirely, as we said in our motion, his choice. But with respect, Your Honours aren't dealing with what if, what may, when, how, but what is the situation today. The situation today -- I can tell Your Honour this -- is if he's released on provisional release to go back to Banja Luka in -- at the moment for a man in his condition, a healthy condition, able to walk, talk, play tennis, do whatever he wants to, Your Honour, that's a very different matter from a man who's on his death bed. We're not talking about a man who is on his death bed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Zecevic, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to what Ms. Korner has stated and also what --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very shortly, Your Honours. First of all, I would like to point out that Rule 65(B) says that the -- the release may be ordered if the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the accused, if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person." So in my mind, the Prosecution's submission should have been whether General Talic's release does pose a danger or not. And that is about everything which I would like to say on this subject. For -- for the further submissions, what my learned colleague has made, I'm -- I'm really in vain, are we supposed to wait -- if I correctly understood, we are supposed to wait that the -- the medical condition of our client deteriorates further, or that it appears that he's on a death bed before we can decide on his motion for provisional release. I have already given our submission to that question and would not like to repeat myself again. For the purposes of this -- of this situation with Banja Luka and Belgrade, the Defence can -- and would like to ask for a leave to amend the motion where we would add the municipality of Belgrade, because one of the Talic's son is living, actually, in Belgrade, and therefore we can -- we can assume that he can stay in the -- in his flat in the municipality of Belgrade for the purposes of -- while undergoing the -- the therapy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Substitute one for the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. But add "Belgrade," because we would not like to -- to substitute the Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But either/or.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Either/or, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to formalise it, or shall we take it as --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you permit us to do it orally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the record, then -- then we should -- we should modify under "relief requested," (A)(i) -- Just bear with me, Your Honours, for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What -- the way I see -- I see it, without making a suggestion as such, is as -- as an alternative, the defendant shall remain within the confines of the -- would it be municipality of Belgrade or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, municipality of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The municipality of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where he would receive the necessary treatment at the military --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- et cetera. But making it clear that if that is the option that is -- is chosen, it would not mean that he is free to go at any time to Banja Luka without first obtaining the authorisation of the Court, of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, it has to be made -- in other words, I would give you time to formulate it in writing, because this is not something --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- That --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think we should do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I would also give -- I would also need to give the Prosecution to respond to that. I mean, the Prosecution has got an idea now of what you may be suggesting as an alternative. And if you feel like -- if you think you can make any submission on that, you're free to do so now or alternatively you can wait for the written amendment and then you can make the submission afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it makes any difference to our suggestion. Your Honour, we're saying that this effectively should be a form of detention in one form or another. The Defence are saying no, it should be provisional release. We're saying -- and whether the detention is such that he remains in detention at his son's flat, which we were unaware of, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm unaware of it too. But it has the advantage, first of all, of possibly eliminating the Banja Luka part of it, and that would put at least -- at least the -- lessen the preoccupations of the Prosecution, which are quite understandable. That's number one. And secondly, in the course of your submissions you did mention at a certain point in time if detention in the military hospital was not possible for a prolonged -- a continuous, uninterrupted, that one could possibly think of a house arrest or something along those lines. And this is why my -- my mind is actually running at this point in time, trying to fit in what Mr. Zecevic has come up with -- with what you had stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I mean, what we're talking about -- I mean, clearly, realistically, if this hospital is the only specialist hospital and he doesn't require to stay there, then there must be somewhere else. But that's -- these are the discussions that have been going on between our office and Mr. Djeric. But Your Honour, if -- what we're talking about at the moment, until the matter has become clarified after he's had the treatment, is detention. And if it's detention in the hospital, plus he is to remain within the confines of his son's flat in Belgrade, then that would content us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, again, this is an addition that you will have to make in the report that your embassy will send to capitol; in other words, if this -- I'm not telling you that this Trial Chamber will come to that conclusion, but for argument's sake, if we came to the conclusion to release General Talic, on condition that he stays under sort of a house arrest in Belgrade, free to attend for medical treatment in the military medical academy in Belgrade, that would still entail a measure of responsibility, supervision, by the authorities in Belgrade. See, in any country -- in Belgrade you have an ordinary person who is put under house arrest, it needs to be monitored, it needs to be supervised. So that is a measure of responsibility and accountability that would fall on the government in Belgrade. So the government in Belgrade would need to be prepared to guarantee that before we can even think of proceeding along those lines. Shall we -- is there anything else anyone would like to -- Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are -- there are three paragraphs under paragraph 7 of the Prosecutor's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a moment until I get the response. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: G, H, and I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which I have some concern about, as counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. I'm going to assume that General Talic is going back to the former Yugoslavia somewhere, and I'm going to assume that one of the things that will happen which should happen and -- must happen, I would suggest, with regard to a person who is dying is that he have an opportunity to see his dearest friends, his closest friends, his old friends, and they have an opportunity to see him. I don't want to face a situation at some point in my trial where the Prosecutor says that a witness that I am proposing to bring here cannot testify because he spoke with General Talic immediately before his death in violation of paragraph H of these conditions. It may very well be that there are a number of people in that category who will wind up coming here as witnesses for Mr. Brdjanin. I can't see any basis, for particularly H and I of that paragraph and certainly if he's not here, he can't have any contact with his co-accused who is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With whom he can have contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With whom he can have contact now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, right. And frequently. So I just don't -- I don't see the basis for those. They don't seem to have anything to do with securing Mr. Talic's situation in Belgrade or wherever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're very clever, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I think Mr. Ackerman better go and read the motion put in on behalf of General Talic by his own counsel, because that repeats "relief requested," paragraphs 4, 5, and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't care who put them in. I'm just telling you that they might impact upon Brdjanin's case. I don't care if they're recommended by Talic's counsel or the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the very -- I'm sorry, that's -- well, our concern is the greatest, that there's a trial going on. He's a party to the trial. He's free, walking the streets of Banja Luka. There are witnesses there. There are witnesses to come. Contact with his co-accused. Thank you very much. Your Honour, those are one of the major concerns which I haven't expressed yet but Mr. Ackerman has brought them up. And I didn't want to mention them because at the moment we're proceeding on a humanitarian basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Any further comments, submissions on this particular matter that you've just referred to, Mr. Ackerman, Madam -- and Ms. Korner? Obviously, I mean -- the conditions -- first of all, there haven't been many orders of provisional release by this Tribunal. There have been some, and the conditions have varied from case to case. There are some which are pretty standard and common to all the orders of provisional release. Definitely Ms. Korner has scored a point in the fact that this is an ongoing trial and during which you may have already indicated who you intend -- or some persons that you intend to call as witnesses. So the accused General Talic is aware of the name, of the identity of those persons. Can I invite you to make submissions on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not the case. And I certainly have -- I understand the Prosecution's position, and I have no objection to an order that would prohibit him from having any contact whatsoever with any one who he knows will be a witness for the Prosecution. But I think that's an entirely different matter. And that's not a problem, and I don't object to that. I'm only concerned that I don't want at some point down the road to have an objection to a witness that I want to call on the grounds that -- that he spoke to General Talic right before his death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one. Talic shall not have any contact with the other co-accused. Now, this, I think, is pretty much something not to worry about. It's one condition which is understandable and I don't think it should create or pose any problems as far as we are concerned. Talic shall not have any contact whatsoever nor in any way interfere with any person who may testify at this trial. Why should Talic be allowed to interfere with any person who may testify at his trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He should never be allowed to interfere with anyone who will testify at his trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is: What trial is it going to be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His trial, we are saying. Because it doesn't say "Brdjanin's trial." It says "his trial."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it's a joint trial, is it his trial or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a joint trial. But that stands to be seen, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you and I wear glasses for a reason, to see further than our nose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. So last one: "Talic shall not discuss his case with anyone other than his counsel." I mean, does it really worry you? Okay. So -- shall we bring -- do you have any further submissions? If not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had a slightly worried note from behind. But as I understand it, Your Honour was saying it could have been read a different way, that the "no contact with his co-accused" was self-evidently one that you would impose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's all right. Don't worry. I just had a very concerned -- from the background. Otherwise, no, Your Honour, I have no further submissions to make on this. Your Honour, I'm come back to when I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we give provision until release or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we may not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all that I'm asking, when we started it off it was whether Your Honours intend to give a ruling in advance of any kind of guarantees from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would have -- I mean, until 12.30, Ms. Korner, we had absolutely no idea of what your reaction, your response would be. Your response posed -- you may sit down. Your response posed a particular problem in the sense that we knew that there would be a representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia here present in court. In a situation where we had a document which made it clear that no guarantees of any sort would be forthcoming before, I would imagine, parliament sits later on this week, and not knowing at the time and before we started the sitting and had the gentleman sitting where he's sitting now, whether he was aware of the contents of your response, because he would still have -- be required to report to his ambassador, first, and then send whatever they usually send to capitol, and then wait for -- wait for that. But we have two options now: We have the first option of accepting outright the motion for provisional release, and that could be accepted with the proviso that would -- we would require all these guarantees and release would be effective once those guarantees are forthcoming. But what you propose entails a different decision. I mean -- and we -- we think it would be extremely out of place to decide, yes, house arrest or yes, detention in the military academy hospital of -- in Belgrade before we even know -- you can't decide these things and say "if they are accepted -- the conditions are accepted, then he is released." I don't know. If you think that we could live with that, I think by tomorrow we should be in a position to reach a decision. But everything would depend on if and when and but. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I perfectly understand that. That's why I was -- I mean, may I apologise for the fact that you only received it at 12.30. I don't think I'm going to quibble over a half an hour or whatever when it was actually handed over. But as we said to you, the reason -- one of the reasons that we asked for the adjournment was the Prosecutor didn't return to this country until yesterday, and we then had to formulate what were her instructions to us. So that's -- that's the reason -- I'm sorry that it was delayed until this morning. Your Honours, as to the progress of the trial, I mean, again there are effectively two options: One is that the trial continues in General Talic's absence with his waiver, which we understand from Mr. Zecevic will be forthcoming. But the problems that Your Honour has already alluded to are huge. If Your Honour is wanting me to make a decision on our position on the options, then I will need to ask Your Honours to rise, because I do need to consult further with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem, Ms. Korner, is that -- that will be a further stage, and I am sure that you will all approach it in the most adequate and in the -- in the most reasonable way. The thing is this, that even -- even if Mr. Zecevic were to stand up now and say General Talic's son is prepared to accept his father in his home, under house arrest conditions, et cetera, I still -- I still want to know what -- what kind of guarantees would be forthcoming from the Federal Republic, because I have -- I have in my career handed down several house arrest orders but in conditions where I know precisely how the regime is going to operate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, yes, I appreciate that. I'm just putting before Your Honour the possibilities of what happens next. The second option is that the trial against General Talic is severed; it becomes a separate trial, and the trial continues against Mr. Brdjanin alone. Now, Your Honour, can I make it absolutely clear, if that is what Your Honours decide will happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could decide that ourselves without --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Without you requesting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. This is Your Honours' decision as to how the trial proceeds from here on in. I want to make it absolutely clear, and I imagine that Mr. Ackerman would do the same, but we will be asking for time to -- because we will have to look at the picture of the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- In a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's obvious. And you will have as much time as you require, because we still have a good number of municipalities, one of which is huge, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are all sorts of administrative matters which I'm not sure if Your Honour wants to deal with them today. For example, firstly -- well, if it goes on against Mr. Brdjanin alone, Your Honour said we can have as much time as we like. Our request would be for a week, as of the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I said "as much time as you like" I didn't mean a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But then we'd be asking because of the loss of time to continue during the week that Your Honours have set aside as a -- as a break. And Your Honour, may have made other plans. I have no doubt Mr. Ackerman will tell you that he has made other plans. So that effectively means a two-week break. The next question is: How long will Your Honours be giving us to conduct this case? Are we going to be given a time limit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will -- if we come to that stage, Ms. Korner, if there is a separation of the two accused, one case being put in deep freeze, the other one continuing, we are fully aware that you need time to sit down and have -- have a -- you have to re-draw your strategy, your evidence, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is quite understandable. That is quite understandable. And it's easier said than done because the way of the -- of the way that the indictment is conceived. I've thought about this over the weekend myself, having a look at the indictment, and I realised that if you come to that, your task is by no means any easier than it is now, and you definitely require time. It's an exercise that can be done as we go along as well because it's an exercise that can be done based on municipality after municipality. So it's -- it's a huge exercise but it can be fazed out over a period of time. I don't see any -- any further options particularly because they are very -- the options would be very limited -- if we decide one way or another -- even if we decide not to -- not to grant provisional release, you're going to face this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in slightly different form, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay, in a slightly different -- and also maybe if not next week, if not next month, it will be the month after. And if not the month after, the month after. When it may be more difficult for you to re-draw your lines and your strategy and -- and aim your guns. You know, I mean, it's -- it's not going to be easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no. I mean, I think -- well, as I say, we're -- the real question is now when Your Honours want to make the decision and will that be Thursday -- or Thursday afternoon, once the Federal Republic has decided on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we could make -- we could take a decision tomorrow morning if we wanted to. Even this evening, if we decided to stay here as long as is necessary. But the thing is that the -- the real uncertainties that we should be talking about is we have a responsibility first towards this -- the -- towards the whole institution, secondly -- although this is in the hierarchical -- what I am saying -- secondly, to the humanitarian rights of the accused; and thirdly, to make sure that whatever we decide can be effectively monitored, can be effectively guaranteed. So when I say so, I do not mean to say that even we doubt for a single minute the guarantees of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but we are not in a position now to know whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is prepared to give those guarantees. This is the only problem that we have, because if -- if not, we would have given down a decision saying one thing or another and then having possibly -- because let's say that we say, "Okay, we go for the option that you gave that, you proposed, detention, pure detention in the military hospital in Belgrade," then on Friday we get a communication from the government of Yugoslavia saying "no way. We are not prepared to undertake -- undertake that." So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would have committed ourselves to an extent already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then what is the option?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, Your Honour, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Send him to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, your, that's what I mean. So Your Honour, therefore, realistically Your Honours cannot make a final decision on this until Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless I have -- or rather, unless we have an indication from your embassy that there is at least one kind of likely response from your government. There is already an indication that there shouldn't be any major problems, if we are talking of the normal guarantees attached to a provisional release order. And that, you could confirm today, even though your parliament has not met as of yet. Perhaps you could go a step further and communicate your report obviously to capitol and come back to us by means of a note verbale or a formal communication, at least equivalent to a letter of intent, giving us an indication that the Yugoslav government would not probably find any objection, say, for example, to detention in the military -- or house arrest, supervision. And also we need to know that the military hospital in Belgrade is prepared to give General -- I mean, I would take it for granted, but we also need to have that kind of indication too. I mean, that should not present, I would imagine, any major problem. But if you are in a position to give us an indication, then we should be in a position perhaps to anticipate whatever decision we need to take and not postpone it until the Yugoslav government has met and decided, and then obviously we would -- we would see what the situation is after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is no doubt that the government planned to issue guarantees for Mr. Talic for provisional release of Mr. Talic. It is no doubt concerning that. But only doubt is concerning the conditions of that guarantee. And I -- I can promise you I will let you -- let you know as soon as possible when I receive any sign from Belgrade about that -- those conditions. This is only -- what can I say in this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that is a diplomat's answer which, in the circumstances, I am prepared to take. And I wouldn't expect you to go beyond -- beyond that. You have been extremely reasonable with this Tribunal, which would like to show its appreciation to you and to your government. The last thing that -- given the situation as it has developed I would like to address, is that it's obvious that we could reach a decision in any of the three ways that I mentioned earlier, either tomorrow or the day after or the day after. In the meantime, we have a duty to ensure that General Talic is not suffering any prejudice to his health, even if he remains -- even if we are talking of a day of detention in the unit here. So what I am going to do is to order the Registrar to communicate with the commandant of the detention unit, who, with the help and/or advice of the medical officer of the unit will approach General Talic and establish whether it is his desire to start undergoing any treatment -- any kind of treatment here in The Hague, pending the decision of this Chamber on the motion for provisional -- on his motion for provisional release. Treatment of any kind will be commenced and given to General Talic in any case, should the medical officer of the unit -- of the detention unit deem it necessary. It should commence outright. Okay? Immediately. The same provision applies if the other intervention that reference is made to -- has been made to by Dr. Valke and the two consultants, has now become necessary as a result of the lapse of a week since they gave testimony. In other words, what I am saying, Madam Chuqing, in case you are asked to explain, is that we had an indication that pleural effusion is already recurring, and this may require two kinds of treatment: Either the extraction of the fluid or the surgical intervention that was mentioned, that is, the gluing of the pleura with the thorax. If either of the two have become necessary, then the Tribunal, the Chamber is drawing the attention of whoever is responsible for the detention unit to have this treatment given to General Talic without any delay. We will not be sitting tomorrow, obviously. However, if anything arises between now and tomorrow which would require us to sit and discuss, please let us know. We will be at your disposal. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Korner raised the issue briefly about what might happen with the trial, and I don't want my silence to foreclose me from speaking to you a little bit about that. So I'll just mention some of the thoughts I've had as quickly as I can right now. I think Your Honour had a moment last week when you understood the profound effect that this might have on the continuation of this trial, and I want to just give you some things to think about in that regard. A little over two years ago we sat together with the lawyers for General Talic and agreed to divide the responsibilities regarding preparation of this case. That meant that I took no responsibility for any of the military aspects of the case. We have not read or paid any attention to speak of to all of the military documents that are in this case, which is probably more than half of the documents that exist. We have not conducted any investigation regarding the military aspects of this case. We have not contacted or arranged for any witnesses regarding the military aspects of this case. I am told by Madam Fauveau that in her considered judgement I'm a year away from being prepared to handle that part of this case. I can't imagine that we would want to delay this case for a year. But I do have a need to get some significant work done to be prepared to handle that part of this case. You will notice that as this case has gone forward, there are certain witnesses that have been basically my responsibility and certain witnesses that have been basically the responsibility of General Talic's team, and that has something to do with the original agreement that we made regarding our responsibilities in that regard. I'm not at liberty to tell you in open court the other things I'm exploring, but it may be that there is a solution that would permit this case to go forward without any delay beyond that which the Prosecutor has suggested, and that will involve a number of things, including negotiations with the Office of the Registrar. If that can be done, then there should be no significant problem. If it cannot, then I suggest to you that there really is a significant problem. And what I can tell you today is that I am working on that, and we are all working on that. But a great deal depends on what Your Honours do with regard to General Talic, as to what -- which way we might jump with regard to that and what might work best for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand you, let's imagine for a moment that there is a separation of the two accused. If I am reading you well, it's importing an element from the back bench to the front bench. Do I read you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That -- that could be a possibility, Your Honour. That's one of the things that we might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- Be able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's call it a day. I can assure you, Mr. Ackerman, that your problems are my problems, and I have more than -- more problems than you have thought of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- may I then, leaving aside Mr. Ackerman's in terrorem suggestions for the moment -- I do want to raise very briefly, because it will have to be adjourned to another time, clearly. And that's the question of the report that appeared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- In a publication which I have never heard of before called Dani. We saw it through the Internet. Your Honours will recall that the Defence for General Talic for obvious reasons were at the stage when this arose very clear that this was to be confidential and therefore any sessions should be in closed session, and we supported them for the same reasons. The report that appeared on Friday, which was taken off the Internet, which Your Honours have copies of and which I provided to Defence counsel, not only stated in terms, in the public that the -- that General Talic had lung cancer, which was discovered accidentally -- and it's clear that this -- there was detail obtained -- medical staff diagnosed liquid in the lungs. It turned out to be metastasis cancer. And according to one of Dani's sources, Dutch doctors gave Talic two more months to live. Now, Your Honour, what concerns us the most is this: Closed session is held so that witnesses who have genuine fears for their safety and security -- and the Chamber has seen the information -- and it doesn't always apply. Quite you have been it applies to Defence witnesses as well -- give evidence in closed session on the basis that they are protected from any of that being revealed to the public. The report went on to state this: "According to what Dani found out at the session held on Wednesday, the future was discussed. Prosecution would like to continue with the trial in absence. Defence agreed to that; however, they do not want to accept Talic's general authorisation." And then it goes on to deal with matters, and it's stated that this was in closed session: "One of the things that caused the most heat in the discussion was Talic's voyage route to Belgrade." Now, Your Honour, the rest is complete unparalleled invented rubbish. But Your Honour, it purports to be a report of what went on in closed session. In any event, it's clear that a lot of published that was held in closed session. Your Honours, I'm inviting Your Honours to have this reporter appear before Your Honours to explain why this report was published, why it purported to give evidence of what was said in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any observations, remarks, submissions? Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we -- we have been informed by -- of this just this -- or just this morning, when Ms. Korner gave us the copy of that. I mean, we are amazed, as Ms. Korner is, because it was us who actually insisted on the closed session because the information in that regard has -- is confidential material, because it deals with the -- with the medical health of our client. Anyhow, we have -- we have been informed that during the press conference there has been a question posed to Mr. Landsdale, as a board parole [sic] of the Tribunal, concerning the same issues, and that is what led us to file the motion to leave the confidentiality, because it is obvious that somehow the information has come to the press of the -- what was said in the closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's very distressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is. Believe me, Your Honours. It's much more distressing to us, concerning the -- the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very distressing, because -- we are in open session now, and I am pleased that we are in open session because I can make a declaration. The only reason why we had a closed session was to enable us to find out the true details of the accused's present state of health, diagnosis and prognosis. At that stage we were committed to guarantee his privacy. Beyond that, I made it clear to all of you that it was our responsibility, having surpassed that stage, to go in open session, because this is -- becomes then something that is public domain and necessary to guarantee transparency of these proceedings. But what appeared in that paper -- I mean, it's -- me too, it's the first time I'm hearing about this publication. I never heard about it before -- is distressing, because it's not a repetition or a fabrication, an elaboration of what was said in the course of the press conference given by Mr. Landsdale. It goes beyond that. There is a part which is true, a part which is speculation, part which is, I would imagine, imagination. I don't know. But it is not fair, because if we can't guarantee that what is confidential and in closed session remains confidential and in closed session, then we have a problem. Then we have a problem. Yes, Ms. Korner, the -- your verbal request will be acted upon by this Tribunal, and the registrar is entrusted with providing this Chamber with the details of who needs to be summoned to appear before this Tribunal. When I say "entrusted," you can communicate --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know the name of the reporter. It may be that the Defence are able to -- I'm told he's been attending this trial regularly, but I have no idea who he is, and I'm told he isn't here today, which doesn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he wasn't here on Friday -- or on Wednesday, when we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He certainly wasn't in court. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't know even -- even the newspaper, less -- and the reporter, of course, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But perhaps you can find out, because obviously I cannot summon ghosts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can give you some information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's very good, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe it was on Wednesday night that -- that I learned that there was a almost full report on Banja Luka Radio about this whole thing, that everyone in Banja Luka had become aware of it by Wednesday night. And my conclusion, which may or may not be right, was that that information must have come out of the detention centre. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even your client is not depicted very nicely in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even your client is not depicted very nicely in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reference to him is not nice at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I did see that. It's not nice. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't like these things. I don't like these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: None of us do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we will be at your disposal tomorrow, if needs be. Councillor, if you are in a position to provide us with a decision tomorrow, pending a final decision on Thursday, please let us know, because we possibly -- you would put us in a position where we could act tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
